doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Discovering Monk and Miles; wartime San Diego music scene
summary: He found the East Coast innovators, saw Ellington live as a kid, and recalls booming San Diego clubs full of Navy and defense-plant crowds and local players.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah, exactly. A lot of people do. They buy their own stampers and literally you can produce CDs at home now, and buy the jewel boxes. So I don’t know. But then shortly after that then I discovered Monk and Miles and the people, the really historic people on the east coast who had changed the face of the music. And I had seen Duke live here when I was still a kid. His band came to town, and I remember seeing Jazz at the Phil, that came through. So you know I’d had some good roots in that area. And there was actually a really thriving music scene in San Diego when I was growing up. I was fortunate, because it was a Navy town and this was the war. San Diego was a jumping town between the service people that were stationed here and all of the people who came out here from all over the country to work in the plants, the aircraft plants and defense, night clubs were booming then and I mean like seven nights a week and Sunday matinees and there were great players here. Harold Land was here at one time, and there’s a wonderful alto player in New York I’ve never met but he’s from San Diego named Arthur Blythe. He’s a marvelous player, I really admire him a lot, and I think he used to work around here in R&B bands, growing up in San Diego. And Walter Fuller was here, a trumpet player who’d been with Lionel Hampton’s band and there were a lot of wonderful players. And so it was a good environment to grow up in. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
